description: Mole Negro Oaxacan Black Mole is a culinary jewel from Oaxaca, Mexico, known for its incredibly rich, complex, and dark sauce. This traditional dish combines a symphony of chiles, spices, nuts, seeds, and chocolate to create a deeply flavorful experience. It is often served with chicken or turkey, making it a truly unforgettable main course for any special occasion.

instructions.title: Prepare Chiles
instructions.text: Toast the dried mulato, pasilla, and ancho chiles in a dry skillet over medium heat for 1-2 minutes until aromatic. Be careful not to burn them. Transfer to a bowl, cover with hot water, and let them soak for 15-20 minutes until softened. Drain and set aside.

instructions.title: Roast Aromatics
instructions.text: While chiles soak, roast the tomatillos, Roma tomatoes, chopped white onion, and peeled garlic cloves in the same dry skillet (or on a baking sheet) until softened and slightly charred, about 5-7 minutes. Set aside to cool slightly.

instructions.title: Toast Nuts and Spices
instructions.text: In the same skillet, toast the almonds, pecans, pumpkin seeds, sesame seeds, Mexican cinnamon stick, whole cloves, black peppercorns, anise seeds, dried thyme, and dried marjoram over medium-low heat. Stir constantly until fragrant, about 3-5 minutes. Do not burn.

instructions.title: Blend Ingredients
instructions.text: Combine the soaked chiles, roasted aromatics, toasted nuts and spices, and sliced ripe plantain (or raisins) in a blender. Add 2 cups of chicken broth. Blend until the mixture is very smooth, adding more broth as needed to achieve a thick, pourable paste. For a finer mole, pass the mixture through a fine-mesh sieve, pressing with a spoon.

instructions.title: Cook the Mole Base
instructions.text: Heat the lard or vegetable oil in a large heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium heat. Carefully add the blended mole paste. Cook, stirring constantly, for at least 15-20 minutes. This crucial step deepens the flavor and darkens the color of the mole.

instructions.title: Simmer and Season
instructions.text: Gradually stir in the remaining 4-6 cups of chicken broth, the Mexican chocolate tablet, sugar, and salt to taste. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook for another 15-20 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the mole thickens to your desired consistency and all flavors have melded. Serve hot with cooked chicken or turkey.

tips: For the deepest flavor, ensure you properly toast the chiles, nuts, and spices without burning them. This step is essential for a rich mole.
If you cant find Mexican chocolate, you can substitute unsweetened baking chocolate with a pinch of cinnamon and sugar to taste.
Mole Negro improves with age. Consider making it a day ahead and gently reheating it; the flavors will meld and deepen even further.
article:
Embark on a culinary journey to the heart of Oaxaca, Mexico, where ancient traditions and vibrant flavors converge to create one of the most revered dishes in Mexican cuisine: Mole Negro. This isn't just a sauce; it's a symphony of tastes, a testament to patience, and a celebration of culture. Often reserved for special occasions, Mole Negro is a rich, complex, and profoundly satisfying dish that captivates the senses with its dark hue and intricate layers of smoky, sweet, spicy, and earthy notes. If you're ready to explore the depths of authentic Mexican dinner recipes, prepare to be enchanted by the magic of Oaxacan Black Mole.

## What is Mole Negro Oaxacan Black Mole?

Mole Negro, meaning "black mole," is arguably the most famous and elaborate of the seven moles of Oaxaca. It’s a culinary masterpiece, known for its distinctively dark color and incredibly complex flavor profile, achieved through a laborious process involving numerous ingredients. Unlike simpler sauces, a true Oaxacan Black Mole can incorporate anywhere from 20 to over 30 components, including several types of dried chiles, nuts, seeds, spices, fruits, and, famously, Mexican chocolate.

The preparation of Mole Negro is not merely cooking; it's an art form passed down through generations. Each ingredient is carefully toasted, fried, or rehydrated to unlock its full potential before being ground into a smooth paste. This paste is then slowly fried in lard and simmered with broth until it reaches a velvety, profound consistency. The resulting sauce is a harmonious blend of smoky heat from the chiles, sweetness from fruits and chocolate, earthiness from nuts and seeds, and warmth from aromatic spices. It’s a dish that embodies the soul of Oaxacan gastronomy, offering a taste experience unlike any other.

## Ingredients You Need

Crafting authentic Oaxacan Black Mole requires a dedicated shopping trip and a pantry stocked with a variety of specialized items. Don't be intimidated by the long list; each ingredient plays a crucial role in building the unparalleled depth of flavor.

**For the Chiles (approx. 150g total):**
* 4-5 large Ancho chiles (dried poblano, smoky, fruity)
* 4-5 large Mulato chiles (dried mulato, sweet, chocolatey)
* 4-5 large Pasilla Oaxaca chiles (dried chilaca, smoky, slightly spicy)
* 2-3 Chipotle chiles (dried smoked jalapeño, for heat and intense smokiness)

**For the Aromatics & Thickeners:**
* 1 medium white onion, roughly chopped
* 6-8 cloves garlic, peeled
* 1 ripe plantain, sliced (for sweetness and body)
* 2 stale corn tortillas, torn
* 1 small bolillo (Mexican bread roll) or slice of white bread, stale
* 1/2 cup raisins
* 1/4 cup prunes, pitted
* 2 tablespoons lard or vegetable oil (for frying)

**For the Nuts & Seeds:**
* 1/2 cup almonds
* 1/4 cup peanuts
* 1/4 cup pepitas (pumpkin seeds)
* 2 tablespoons sesame seeds, plus more for garnish

**For the Spices:**
* 1 teaspoon whole black peppercorns
* 1/2 teaspoon whole cloves
* 1/2 teaspoon cumin seeds
* 1 small stick true cinnamon (Canela), about 2 inches
* 1/4 teaspoon anise seeds (optional, for subtle licorice notes)

**For the Finishing:**
* 100g Mexican chocolate (tabletas, often includes cinnamon and sugar)
* 6-8 cups chicken or vegetable broth, hot
* Salt to taste
* 1-2 tablespoons sugar (if needed, to balance flavor)
* Extra lard or vegetable oil for frying the paste

## Step-by-Step Instructions

Making Oaxacan Black Mole is a labor of love, but the process is incredibly rewarding. Take your time, enjoy each step, and savor the evolving aromas.

**Step 1: Prepare the Chiles**
Remove stems and seeds from all dried chiles. Open them flat. In a dry comal or skillet over medium-low heat, toast the chiles for 30-60 seconds per side until fragrant and slightly pliable, being careful not to burn them (burnt chiles will make the mole bitter). Immediately place toasted chiles in a bowl and cover with very hot water. Let them rehydrate for 20-30 minutes until soft. Reserve the soaking liquid.

**Step 2: Toast and Fry Other Ingredients**
In a large skillet or Dutch oven, heat 2 tablespoons of lard or oil over medium heat.
* **Fry Aromatics:** Add chopped onion and garlic, cook until softened and lightly browned, about 5-7 minutes. Remove and set aside.
* **Fry Plantain & Bread:** Fry plantain slices until golden brown. Remove. Fry tortillas and bread until crisp. Remove.
* **Toast Nuts & Seeds:** In the same skillet (without adding more fat), toast almonds, peanuts, pepitas, and sesame seeds separately until golden and fragrant. Watch carefully, as they burn easily. Remove and set aside.
* **Toast Spices:** Briefly toast peppercorns, cloves, cumin seeds, cinnamon, and anise seeds (if using) for about 30 seconds until aromatic. Do not burn.

**Step 3: Blend the Paste**
Drain the rehydrated chiles, reserving the soaking liquid. In a high-speed blender, combine the softened chiles, fried onion and garlic, fried plantain, fried tortillas and bread, toasted nuts and seeds, raisins, prunes, and toasted spices. Add about 2-3 cups of the reserved chile soaking liquid (or chicken broth) to help the blending process. Blend until you achieve a very smooth, thick paste. This may require blending in batches and stopping to scrape down the sides. If necessary, pass the paste through a fine-mesh sieve for an even silkier texture, though a powerful blender often makes this unnecessary.

**Step 4: Fry the Mole Paste**
This is a critical step for developing the deep flavor and color of your Oaxacan Black Mole. In your large Dutch oven or a heavy-bottomed pot, heat 3-4 tablespoons of fresh lard or oil over medium-high heat until shimmering. Carefully add the mole paste (it will splatter!). Reduce heat to medium-low and cook the paste, stirring constantly, for at least 20-30 minutes, or even longer. The paste will darken significantly, thicken, and release its oils, developing a rich, caramelized aroma. This slow frying deepens the flavor profile immensely.

**Step 5: Simmer and Finish**
Once the paste is deeply fried, gradually stir in the hot chicken or vegetable broth, about 1 cup at a time, incorporating it fully before adding more. Bring the mole to a gentle simmer. Add the Mexican chocolate, stirring until it is completely melted and incorporated. Continue to simmer the mole uncovered for at least 45 minutes to 1.5 hours, stirring occasionally to prevent sticking. The sauce should thicken to a rich, velvety consistency, similar to a creamy soup. If it gets too thick, add more broth.

**Step 6: Season and Rest**
Taste the Oaxacan Black Mole and adjust seasoning with salt. If it tastes too bitter or too spicy, add a tablespoon or two of sugar to balance the flavors. The mole should be a perfect balance of sweet, savory, spicy, and earthy. Allow the mole to rest for at least 30 minutes before serving, or even better, prepare it a day in advance as the flavors deepen overnight.

## Pro Tips for the Best Results

*   **Quality Ingredients are Key:** The success of your Oaxacan Black Mole hinges on fresh, high-quality ingredients, especially the chiles. Seek out specialty Mexican markets for the best selection.
*   **Don't Burn the Chiles:** This is the most common pitfall. Toast them until fragrant and pliable, but never until smoking or charred, which will impart a bitter taste.
*   **Smoothness is Paramount:** Invest time in blending the paste until it's incredibly smooth. A gritty mole detracts from the luxurious texture. Strain it if your blender isn't powerful enough.
*   **Patience with Frying the Paste:** This step transforms the flavor. Don't rush it. The longer and more slowly you fry the paste, the deeper and richer your mole will become.
*   **Balance the Flavors:** Taste, taste, taste! The goal is harmony. Adjust salt, sugar, and even a touch more broth if needed. The flavors should be complex but balanced, with no single element overpowering the others.
*   **Make it Ahead:** Mole Negro benefits greatly from resting. Prepare it a day or two in advance and gently reheat it before serving. The flavors meld and deepen beautifully.

## Serving Suggestions

Oaxacan Black Mole is traditionally served with poultry, most commonly shredded chicken or turkey. The rich, dark sauce beautifully complements the mild flavor of the meat.

*   **Classic Pairing:** Ladle generous amounts of mole over shredded chicken or turkey pieces.
*   **Accompaniments:** Serve alongside fluffy Mexican red rice or plain white rice to soak up the exquisite sauce. Warm corn tortillas are essential for scooping up every last drop.
*   **Garnish:** A sprinkle of toasted sesame seeds and perhaps a few sprigs of fresh cilantro add a lovely visual and textural contrast.
*   **Beyond Poultry:** While traditional, mole negro also pairs wonderfully with pork shoulder, duck, or even as a sauce for tamales or enchiladas. For a vegetarian option, try it over roasted sweet potatoes, portobello mushrooms, or hearty black beans.

## Variations and Substitutions

While the recipe above aims for an authentic Oaxacan Black Mole, there's room for personalization and adaptation based on availability and preference.

*   **Chile Combinations:** Experiment with different chile ratios. For more heat, add a few more chipotles or a small arbol chile. For a milder mole, reduce the chipotle. Some recipes include chilhuacle negro chiles, which are very specific to Oaxaca and highly prized for their deep, earthy notes.
*   **Nut & Seed Choices:** While almonds, peanuts, and pepitas are standard, you can also incorporate walnuts, pecans, or even hazelnuts for different flavor nuances.
*   **Sweeteners:** Instead of granulated sugar, consider using piloncillo (Mexican brown sugar cones) for a more authentic, caramel-like sweetness.
*   **Chocolate:** Authentic Mexican chocolate is highly recommended due to its unique blend of cacao, sugar, and cinnamon. If unavailable, use a high-quality dark chocolate (70-80% cacao) and add a pinch of cinnamon and a touch more sugar.
*   **Vegetarian/Vegan:** To make this Oaxacan Black Mole vegetarian or vegan, simply use vegetable broth instead of chicken broth and vegetable oil instead of lard for frying. Serve it over roasted vegetables, plant-based proteins, or hearty grains.
*   **Simplification:** While this recipe is for a scratch-made mole, commercially prepared mole pastes are available for a quicker option. However, they won't quite capture the nuanced depth of a homemade Oaxacan Black Mole.

Creating Mole Negro is a rewarding culinary adventure that connects you to centuries of Mexican tradition. It's an investment of time and effort, but the resulting depth of flavor and the joy of sharing such a magnificent dish make every step worthwhile. Dive in, embrace the process, and discover why Oaxacan Black Mole is truly one of the world's great culinary treasures.
